clue.text: Place to ruminate clue for 'ewer'?

parts.note: the first three letters inside the quotes spell a ewe, and a ewe is a female of the flock
the letter left at the end is R, cricket's abbreviation for a single score

explanation.surface: Somewhere quiet to sit and mull over how you might go about cluing the word 'ewer'.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is itself a cryptic clue, and reading it as one spells the quoted word. Ruminants chew the cud, so 'ruminate' is pointing at grazing animals rather than at thinking.
explanation.definitionFit: A sheep run is a stretch of grazing land a flock is turned out on, and sheep are ruminants — so it is literally a place to ruminate.

clue.text: See 10 Across
See 12 Across
One colour only — second one not included

indicators.note: Something included in a package is carried along inside it, so this word is planted between the two pieces around it.

parts.note: a mo is a moment — 'half a mo' — which is a second in the loose sense
likewise taken as written
the word goes in whole, exactly as it stands

explanation.surface: A price quoted for a single colour, with the second item excluded from the deal.
explanation.walkthrough: The dash reads as a dealer's small print and 'second one not included' as the exclusion clause. Read as instructions, 'included' does the opposite job — it puts something in.
explanation.definitionFit: Monotone describes something carried out in a single colour or shade throughout, with no variation from end to end.

clue.text: Resort to cornmeal unfortunately

indicators.note: An unfortunate turn of events leaves things in a state nobody arranged, which is what happens to these letters.

parts.note: anagram fodder, ten letters

explanation.surface: Somebody down on their luck having to fall back on cornmeal for dinner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Resort to' reads as one phrase — falling back on something — and the definition is only the first word of it. The 're-sort' buried in that word is the setter's wink.
explanation.definitionFit: Monte Carlo is the casino quarter of Monaco on the Riviera, a place people travel to for pleasure — a resort in the holiday sense.

clue.text: Peninsula of Palermo — if rock climbing regularly

indicators.note: In a down clue, climbing runs from the foot of the entry towards the top, so the letters are read the other way up.
Regular means at a fixed interval rather than at every step, so only every second letter is picked up.

parts.note: the second, fourth, sixth, eighth, tenth and twelfth letters of this run of words

explanation.surface: A regular rock-climbing trip on the headland somewhere near Palermo.
explanation.walkthrough: Palermo sits on Sicily, an island, so 'Peninsula of Palermo' cannot be the definition it pretends to be — the town is in the clue only to lend letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The Crimea is the diamond-shaped peninsula hanging off the northern coast of the Black Sea.

clue.text: Its application could help you get into Oxford?

definitions.meaning: The reading the surface pushes is a university application — the form you fill in and post off.

definitions.text: could help you get into Oxford?
definitions.meaning: The reading the setter means is physical: an Oxford is a plain lace-up, and getting into one is a matter of a tight heel.

explanation.surface: A hopeful student wondering what might improve their chances of a place at the university.
explanation.walkthrough: Oxford is a style of lace-up shoe as well as a university, and 'application' slides from a form you send off to a tool you press into use.
explanation.definitionFit: A shoehorn is the smooth curved blade you slip behind your heel to ease a tight shoe on, and an Oxford is a shoe.

clue.text: See 15 Across
Understood our son's bedding smells

indicators.note: Something bedded into a surface lies embedded within it, so the letters sit unbroken inside the words around them.

parts.note: six consecutive letters run from the tail of the first word, straight through the second and into the third

explanation.surface: A family agreeing that their son's bedclothes have started to smell.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s reads as an ordinary possessive, and the letters run straight on through it, which is what makes this span so hard to see.
explanation.definitionFit: Odours are smells — the neutral noun for whatever the nose picks up, though it leans towards the unpleasant end.

clue.text: House band feature in saloon

parts.note: a stately home in the country is known by a four-letter word that also means something to sit on
a band running round something

explanation.surface: The resident band that plays most nights in a bar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'House band' is one phrase in the surface and two separate pieces in the wordplay, and 'saloon' is a body style of car rather than a drinking den.
explanation.definitionFit: A saloon is the standard enclosed four-door car, and a seat belt is one of the fittings every one of them carries.

clue.text: Early on, I go to party with deviant I'd met

indicators.note: To party is to let loose and mix freely, and letters told to do that will not stay in the order they were given.
Something deviant departs from the expected pattern, which is what these letters do to the sequence they arrive in.

parts.note: anagram fodder, five letters
anagram fodder, five letters

explanation.surface: The speaker setting off early for a party in the company of an oddball they had run into before.
explanation.walkthrough: Two anagrams sit side by side and neither indicator announces itself: 'to party' is the invitation the whole surface is built on, and 'deviant' is the odd guest.
explanation.definitionFit: In good time means with time still in hand rather than at the last minute, which is the sense of early wanted here — ahead of schedule.

clue.text: Finish, as elements of Marie Curie's typical description are transposed?

indicators.note: to transpose is to swap the order, so the two halves of the description change places

parts.note: Marie Curie is usually described as a Polish-French physicist: born in Poland, she worked and took citizenship in France

explanation.surface: The biography of Marie Curie ends with a question over how her nationality should be stated.
explanation.walkthrough: Marie Curie was born in Warsaw and became a French citizen, so she is called Polish-French; 'elements' are her description's two words (and nods to her chemistry), which are swapped round.
explanation.definitionFit: French polish is a glossy shellac finish applied to fine wooden furniture.

clue.text: Family group putting down first part of table setting?

indicators.note: The instruction places this piece at the head of the answer, ahead of the two clued before it.

parts.note: the nap of a fabric is its down — the soft pile raised on velvet or baize
your kin are your family
a ring is a group acting together, as in a smuggling ring

explanation.surface: A household laying the table, beginning with the very first thing they set down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Family group' reads as one phrase and is two separate pieces, and 'down' is the fabric word here — the pile on velvet — not a direction.
explanation.definitionFit: A napkin ring is the little band each rolled napkin is threaded through, one of the small objects laid out in a formal table setting.

clue.text: Warship covered by press

parts.note: to press a shirt is to iron it
clad means clothed or covered over

explanation.surface: A naval vessel getting plenty of coverage in the newspapers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Covered by press' reads as newspaper attention; the press here is the household appliance and 'covered' is the clothing word.
explanation.definitionFit: An ironclad was the mid-Victorian warship built of wood and sheathed in iron armour plate, so the word names the ship itself.

clue.text: Turning on Paganini number to begin — as motivation for fitness class?

indicators.note: to begin says this piece comes at the start
turning letters round reorders them, so these are rearranged

explanation.surface: A violin piece by Paganini played to get a fitness class going.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram of ON PAGANINI gives PAIN NO GAIN.
explanation.definitionFit: The slogan says that progress in exercise only comes with effort and discomfort, a gym instructor's motivational line.

clue.text: Cambridge university worried boring papers will be copied

indicators.note: To bore is to drill a hole through something, so what is boring ends up right inside the word it attacks.

parts.note: your ID is the papers that prove who you are
the Massachusetts Institute of Technology stands in Cambridge, Massachusetts
what eats at you is what worries you — 'what's eating him?'

explanation.surface: An anxious Cambridge academic ploughing through a pile of dull papers.
explanation.walkthrough: The Cambridge in play is the Massachusetts one, and 'boring' means drilling rather than dull — two misreadings the surface works hard to keep in place.
explanation.definitionFit: Imitated and copied are plain synonyms; imitating leans towards reproducing a manner or style, copying towards duplicating a thing.

clue.text: Ferraris and Rolls are mostly stolen for joy rides?

indicators.note: the shortened word is taken away from the car name, as if pinched

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: most of the word is kept, its final letter dropped

parts.note: taken as written
to roll something along is to wheel it, so rolls means wheels

explanation.surface: Luxury cars get nicked by joyriders.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ferraris and Rolls' looks like a list of supercars (Rolls being a Rolls-Royce), but Rolls is the verb. 'mostly' cuts 'are' to AR, which is 'stolen' from FERRARIS to leave FERRIS.
explanation.definitionFit: A Ferris wheel is a big fairground wheel ridden purely for pleasure, hence a 'joy ride'.

clue.text: Appropriate clubs potentially qualified

indicators.note: Clubs are only one of four, so the word says to move up from the instance to the class it belongs to.

parts.note: clubs is one of the four suits in a pack of cards
someone able is qualified to do the job

explanation.surface: A set of golf clubs that might just turn out to be good enough.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clubs' is a card suit rather than golf equipment, and 'potentially' is the small word doing the lifting from example to category.
explanation.definitionFit: Suitable and appropriate are near-exact synonyms, both saying a thing fits the occasion, with 'appropriate' the more formal of the pair.

clue.text: See 17 Across
Stayed over in Soho — oddly it's diabolical

indicators.note: Something turned over ends up the other way round, so the word in front of it is read backwards.
Odd counts positions here rather than describing behaviour: the first, third and fifth letters are the ones taken.

parts.note: somebody who stayed in a place lived there
the first, third and fifth letters of these two words

explanation.surface: Someone who spent the night in Soho reporting that, strangely, the experience was dreadful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stayed over' reads as spending the night, which is exactly where the clue wants you, and the little word 'in' is not scenery — it is lending letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Devilish and diabolical both mean 'of the devil', and both have drifted into everyday use for anything fiendishly difficult.

clue.text: Appear upset about King supporting Eastern Arabic rulers

indicators.note: in a down clue the supporting piece sits below, so the rest comes after E
about means around, so the reversed word goes round the letter for king
upset in a down clue means turned upside down, so the word is reversed

parts.note: seem means appear
R is Rex, Latin for king

explanation.surface: Arab rulers seem upset when a king backs the East.
explanation.walkthrough: SEEM reversed gives MEES, which goes around R to make MEERS, with E on top.
explanation.definitionFit: Emeers is a variant spelling of emirs, Muslim rulers in Arab lands.

clue.text: Template censor used after identifying code

indicators.note: 'After' fixes the running order, so the piece it governs follows the other rather than leading.

parts.note: the small file a website leaves on your machine so it recognises you next time
a censor's work is snipping material out

explanation.surface: An official blanking out material once a piece of code has identified it.
explanation.walkthrough: Both halves read as modern office language — the tracking file and the censor's shears — while the definition is quietly asking for a kitchen object.
explanation.definitionFit: A cookie cutter is the shaped tin pressed into rolled dough so that every biscuit comes out identical, which makes it a template in the literal sense.

clue.text: See 22 Across
Fresh investment in Arsenal meant changes on wing at kick-off

indicators.note: at kick-off places these pieces at the start

parts.note: re means on, concerning
an arm is a wing of an organisation

indicators.note: changes means the letters are altered in order

explanation.surface: A football report: Arsenal's new money brought changes on the wing from the start.
explanation.walkthrough: Arsenal looks like the football club, but here it is a store of weapons.
explanation.definitionFit: Rearmament is building up weapons again, refilling a nation's stockpile of arms.

clue.text: Perhaps Leo Sayer's trying another rewrite — initially with chorus moving note lower

indicators.note: initially picks the first letter of each of those words
the note, N, is moved lower down the word, after the G

parts.note: to chorus is to sing together

explanation.surface: Leo Sayer, the 1970s singer, attempts a new version of a song with a revised chorus.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leo Sayer' reads as the pop singer; only 'Leo' is the definition. SING with its N moved below the G gives SIGN.
explanation.definitionFit: Leo is one of the twelve signs of the zodiac, an example of a star sign.

clue.text: See 24 Across
Less important call when 14

parts.note: 14 across is a word meaning clad in iron, and Fe is iron's chemical symbol
to call a friend is to ring them

explanation.surface: Deciding which phone call matters less when someone is at number 14, as if ranking callers by house number.
explanation.walkthrough: The cross-reference is an instruction and not just a source of letters: 14 across means clad in iron, so iron's chemical symbol wraps itself round the other piece.
explanation.definitionFit: Fringe as a modifier means out at the edge of the main event — fringe theatre, fringe politics — so it reads as less important than the centre.

clue.text: Supreme influencer leaving a little something out

indicators.note: a little of the word is its first letter
out signals the letters are put out of their order

explanation.surface: A top influencer quits, leaving a small thing out.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram is of LEAVING plus S.
explanation.definitionFit: Svengali, from du Maurier's novel Trilby, is a person who exerts controlling influence over another.
